If I have a number that represents the design for a building or a mathematical theorem, these numbers have purpose. If I input these numbers to a computer along with some building design software or a copy of Mathematica they
will do something interesting; allowing a construction firm to build a innovative building or a mathematician to check a theorem is sound.

It's a lot harder to prove numbers representing art are functionally useful. A work of art is in some sense not complete — it still needs to go through the process of being appreciated by someone. We could show it to a friend or exhibit it in a gallery but this is un unpredictable process.

Art or Information

Monster poem is almost pure gibberish, but it's undoubtedly art. Art is a tricky problem but, in practice, most of us agree on what constitutes good and bad art. We will look again at art, in Chapter 10.

Classically we assume knowledge is discovered through random chance and iteration. To understand how this might work let's lay out the world's information in a way we can visualize. Imagine every piece of discoverable knowledge could be found in an infinitely large library.
